clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in CYP24A1, encoding 24-hydroxylase, the main enzyme that inactivates 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Loss of this catabolic pathway leaves vitamin D metabolites unopposed, causing hypercalcaemia when vitamin D intake or sun exposure rises
Classically presents in infants after routine vitamin D supplementation with failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration, irritability, polyuria, and hypotonia
Biochemistry shows hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, suppressed parathyroid hormone, and an inappropriately normal or high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
A helpful clue is a low or undetectable 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D with a raised ratio of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis are common, and milder forms may first present in adults with stones
Management centres on strict avoidance of vitamin D supplementation and sun/dietary calcium reduction, with hydration and hypercalcaemia treatment during crises
reference.pathophysiology: CYP24A1 encodes 24-hydroxylase, which initiates the catabolism of both 25-hydroxyvitamin D and active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D into inactive metabolites, providing the principal off-switch for vitamin D signalling. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish this degradation, so active vitamin D metabolites persist and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D remains inappropriately normal or elevated. Unopposed vitamin D action increases intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption, producing hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, and suppressed parathyroid hormone. The excess filtered calcium promotes nephrocalcinosis and stone formation. Because the defect is one of clearance, disease is often unmasked when exogenous vitamin D (as supplements or sunlight) increases substrate, explaining the classic onset after infant prophylaxis.
additionalDifferentials: Williams syndrome and other syndromic infantile hypercalcaemia
Granulomatous disease with extrarenal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone (suppressed)
24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and the 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D ratio as a functional marker
Renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and stones
CYP24A1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with dehydration and lethargy in an infant
Recurrent nephrolithiasis, including first presentation in adulthood
Hypercalcaemic crisis precipitated by vitamin D supplementation
reference.prognosis: With early recognition, withdrawal of vitamin D, and calcium moderation, acute hypercalcaemia resolves and children usually thrive; long-term prognosis depends on the extent of nephrocalcinosis and any resulting renal impairment.
pitfalls: Continuing routine vitamin D supplementation, which perpetuates hypercalcaemia in these patients
Overlooking the diagnosis in an adult stone-former with suppressed parathyroid hormone
Not measuring 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or the diagnostic metabolite ratio
Attributing the hypercalcaemia to vitamin D overdose alone without genetic testing
management: Withdraw all vitamin D supplementation and moderate dietary calcium as the mainstay, since disease is unmasked by exogenous vitamin D substrate
Advise sensible sunlight avoidance to reduce endogenous vitamin D synthesis
Treat acute symptomatic hypercalcaemia with isotonic saline rehydration and a loop diuretic to promote calciuresis
Consider glucocorticoids or an antiresorptive bisphosphonate for refractory hypercalcaemia to curb intestinal absorption and bone resorption
Monitor serum and urinary calcium, parathyroid hormone and renal function, with renal ultrasound surveillance for nephrocalcinosis and stones
Maintain adequate long-term hydration to reduce hypercalciuria and stone formation
Refer to metabolic bone and clinical genetics services and offer genetic counselling with family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Escalate to nephrology for progressive nephrocalcinosis or declining renal function
